# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the strongest document in the series. It registers its mediation analysis before outcomes were available, adds an hours measure that captures unclaimed work, reports the counter arm's closure plainly, and answers both earlier critiques with the right kind of evidence. **Its arithmetic is consistent, but several figures and claims need tightening:** the Summary's decline figure, the control-arm contamination from month 15, what the log measure actually counts, and the word "confirms."

## Arithmetic check

These figures are correct:

- **Varden, timesheet basis.** Output per employee of 0.966 divided by an hours ratio of 0.88 gives +9.8%.
- **Varden, log basis.** 0.966 divided by 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden subset.** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%), and 96.8 / 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Size of the decline.** Going from 12.5% to 9.8% is a fall of 22%. That is "about a quarter," as Section 5 says.

## 1. The Summary overstates the decline

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." That compares a timesheet figure with a log-based figure. The like-for-like comparison, which the body uses, is 12.5% to 9.8%. Mixing the measures makes the decline look larger: about 32% instead of about 22%. The Summary should use 9.8%, or report both measures at 24 months.

## 2. Control offices changed practice from month 15

Two control offices cancelled standing meetings in month 15, after the nine-month report had publicised the meetings finding. This is more than an aside: it changes the control arm.

- **The decline may partly reflect control offices improving.** If two of seven control offices raised output per hour by about 4% from month 15, the treated-versus-control gap narrows for that reason alone. Some of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore be the control arm improving rather than the effect wearing off.
- **This bears on the anti-novelty argument.** It weakens the use of the decline in Section 5, while strengthening the case that the effect hasn't decayed much.

The fix is a sensitivity analysis that excludes the two offices, or one that ends the comparison at month 15. The paper should also say whether the audit was prompted by the published nine-month findings. If it was, that is spillover between arms, which office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

The 4.1% figure for those two offices is a comparison with their own previous six months. Comparing them with the other five control offices over the same period would be easy and much more convincing.

There is also a small consistency check. The average control-arm meeting time moved only from 7.2 to 7.0 hours. If two of seven offices fell by 2.1 hours, the other five must have *risen* by about 0.56 hours on average. That may be true, but it is worth confirming.

## 3. What the log measure counts, and why it matters

The paper describes log-in time as recording "time staff are working on cases." If it counts only case work and excludes meetings, the figures don't fit together:

| | Timesheet hours (relative) | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | ~37.9 | 7.0 | ~30.9 |
| Treated | ~33.4 (−12%) | 3.9 | ~29.5 |

Non-meeting time falls by only about 4.5%. A measure of case-work time alone should fall by about that much, not by 11%. So either:

- log-in time includes meetings, because staff stay logged in during them; or
- some of the figures need reconciling.

The answer matters for two reasons:

- **It affects what the main estimate means.** If log hours include idle or meeting time, "output per log-measured hour" doesn't mean what the paper implies.
- **It bears on the meetings finding.** Output per non-meeting hour rises by only about 1% (0.966 / 0.955). On this simple accounting, removed meeting time could explain most of the per-hour gain, not 47%. The mediation model can legitimately give a lower figure, for example if meetings produced some output. Even so, the paper should explain the gap between the two.

The paper should also say whether there is a pre-trial baseline for the log measure. A difference-in-differences estimate on logs at 24 months needs one, and the table shows no 9-month log figure.

## 4. Mediation: "confirms" overstates what the analysis can show

The registered analysis is a real improvement, but four issues limit what it establishes:

- **The data may overlap with the data that generated the hypothesis.** The meetings hypothesis came from this trial's months 1–9. If the "office-months" in the registered analysis include those months, the test partly reuses the data that produced the hypothesis. The test would be cleaner on months 10–24 only, or the paper should report how the results change when months 1–9 are dropped.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not the office-months.** Office-months within an office aren't independent. The CIs (28–66% and 2–34%) need to account for clustering, ideally with small-sample corrections, as I suggested for the nine-month analysis.
- **The mediators weren't randomised.** Offices whose managers cut meetings most may also have improved other processes. The Limitations name the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption, but the Summary's "confirms" ignores it. "Is consistent with" or "supports" would be accurate.
- **The mediators are linked.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. Shares that add up to 100% (47 + 18 + 35) imply additive, independent pathways. The paper should state how the model handles the relationship between mediators.

The baseline meeting figure (7.4 hours) is new; the nine-month report had only month-6 calendar data. The paper should say how the baseline was obtained, for example from retrieved historical calendars.

## 5. Halden at 24 months: weaker than it looks

- **No comparison group over two years.** A before-after comparison over two years is more exposed to outside trends than one over six months. General productivity growth, new software and process changes during 2023–25 would all appear as "effect." The caveat about survivors is good, but this is a separate and probably larger problem.
- **The response is selective.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. The 11 continuing organisations aren't the 17 in the re-analysis, so comparing 11.8% with that comment's 10.8% says nothing about decay.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the coverage explanation.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But a marketing agency is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding, and it cited client deadlines, not opening hours. That is a counterexample to the clean discretionary/coverage split, and the paper should say so.

## 6. The counter-arm cost figure needs its derivation

Restoring service with 12% more staff, while handling roughly the same number of contacts, would raise cost per contact by about 12%, not 9%. A 9% rise implies about 3% more contacts handled, perhaps through fewer abandoned calls and repeat contacts. That is plausible, but the calculation should be shown.

## 7. The rebuttals

- **Against "entirely an artifact."** The rebuttal is fair. The Varden estimate meets the standards the re-analysis itself recommended. Two qualifications:
  - The estimate is from a single employer with 14 offices.
  - About half the gain may come from reorganisation. That gain is real but not necessarily caused by the hours cut, as the paper's own unplanned observation shows.
- **Against the meta-analysis's "no decay."** The rebuttal is correct and decisive: all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which supports my earlier critique of that review. However, "the gain declined by about a quarter" in one controlled study is still only one study. The trajectory between 9 and 24 months is also unreported. Results at 12 and 18 months would show whether the gain is levelling off or still falling, and the paper shouldn't imply either.
- **Conflict of interest.** R. Okafor is a Halden author, so the follow-up includes the pilot's original authors evaluating their own pilot while rebutting a re-analysis of it. The Varden authors are also the main source of the evidence used to settle the dispute. Neither is disqualifying, but both should be disclosed explicitly.

## Smaller points

- **Overtime cost is still unreported.** Timesheet hours of about 33.4 against a 30-hour schedule imply about 3.4 hours a week of claimed overtime, on top of full pay. Cost per case closed has probably risen by more than 10%. The county reported cost for the counter arm but not for case processing.
- **Sick days are still per FTE.** The −27% figure needs adjusting for exposure (per scheduled day), as before.
- **Resignations have no CI.** The 4.1% v 7.9% comparison still lacks an interval.
- **A low reversion threshold.** The three reverting organisations had output indices of 88–91 when they reverted. That is useful evidence that organisations reverted at fairly modest output losses, and it could be stated as such.

## Overall

The follow-up substantially settles the series. There is a real, durable but declining per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% in backlog-type public-sector work, under rigorous measurement. A large part of it is plausibly linked to meeting reduction. Coverage-bound work could not sustain reduced hours without extra staff. The key revisions before publication are:

- use the like-for-like 9.8% in the Summary;
- run a sensitivity analysis for the control offices' meeting audit;
- define what the log measure counts and reconcile it with the meeting-time arithmetic;
- restrict or check the mediation data to avoid reusing months 1–9, with cluster-appropriate inference;
- replace "confirms" with "supports."
